study.title: Songs 6 - The unique beauty of the beloved and the desired reunion
study.overview: The chapter continues the poetic dialogue between the beloved, the young women of Jerusalem and the beloved. At first, the companions ask where the beloved is, and the answer of the beloved suggests an already restored intimacy, described in garden language and spices. Then the beloved makes a new compliment to her beauty, repeating and enlarging images already used before: she is compared to beautiful cities, to the splendour of dawn, the moon and the sun, and is presented as unique among many other women. The chapter ends with an invitation to return and be contemplated, while the last verse maintains the idea of public admiration for its grace and movement.

outline.title: Search and answer about the beloved
outline.explanation: The young women ask where the beloved was, and the beloved answers that he is in his garden, between spices and lilies. Language suggests closeness and mutual belonging, culminating in confession: it is his, and he is hers.

outline.title: The incomparable beauty of the beloved
outline.explanation: The beloved describes the beloved with a series of poetic comparisons, highlighting his beauty, grace and strength of presence. The description also presents it as unique and more desirable than any other women mentioned in the poetic picture.

outline.title: Garden, movement and final invitation
outline.explanation: There is a scene of displacement to the garden of walnut trees, in poetic language that points to desire and encounter. The chapter closes with the request for the Sulamita to return, in order to be observed in her graceful dance, which reinforces the collective admiration for her.

study.context: The notes received treat the chapter as part of a poem with dialogue between the beloved, the girls and the beloved. A reading suggested in the notes understands that the scene should not be read as a literal event, but as a poetic language of desire and intimacy. References to Tirzah and Jerusalem are used as images of beauty and prestige, without the chapter explaining for itself more historical details.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter values the committed and exclusive love: the phrase I am of my beloved, and my beloved is my own express mutual belonging and affective alliance. Poetry also affirms the uniqueness of the beloved without erasing the surrounding community; she is admired by the young women, queens and concubines, but remains unique in the eyes of the beloved. Comparisons with cities, stars and armies do not seem mere ornamental, but a way to declare that true love sees beauty, dignity and strength in the loved one. In evangelical reading, this can be received as a picture of fidelity, reciprocal admiration and the value of conjugal love, without forcing the text to teach more than it says.

scholarViews.insight: The young women of Jerusalem ask where the beloved was, and the answer of the beloved uses the image of the garden and the lilies to express loving intimacy; the note understands this as a description of sexual intimacy in poetic language.
The request "Volta, Sulamita" is understood as an invitation addressed to Solomon's recognized wife, and the name is seen as a female form linked to the name of Solomon.

questions: What do confession I am of my beloved, and my beloved is my lover teaching about belonging and fidelity in the relationship?
Why does the poet use so many different images to describe the beauty of the beloved rather than a direct description?
How to avoid reading this chapter only as a human novel, without losing the strength of its affective and community language?
study.practice: Notice how the chapter unites desire, admiration and commitment. In practical terms, he invites couples and families to value the exclusivity, sincere praise and the beauty of the other without vulgarity. It also challenges the reader to speak of love with dignity, recognizing that well-chosen words can honor the beloved person. If the text is read in a devotional way, it can inspire gratitude for the fidelity and beauty of love that does not disperse in empty comparisons.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are limited and do not allow the historical sense of expressions such as "Suplam," nor definitively identify the scenario of "carriages of my noble people" or the final expression about "two companies." Tyndale's note suggests that the poem describes intimacy in symbolic language, but this remains interpretation, not absolute textual certainty. It is also not possible to determine with certainty only by the notes, whether the chapter should be read as dreamlike scene, poetic memory or continuous literary staging.
